title: N.L. fisheries minister stayed in Scottish castle, ‘luxury’ shooting lodge on aquaculture giant’s dime
summary: Newfoundland and Labrador’s NDP says the province’s fisheries minister put himself in a “brutal” conflict of interest when he stayed in a castle, then a “luxury” shooting lodge — all on the dime of…

image.caption: Newfoundland and Labrador's Fisheries Minister Loyola O'Driscoll, photographed in front of Confederation Building in St. John's in 2024. (Facebook/Loyola O'Driscoll)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

Newfoundland and Labrador’s NDP says the province’s fisheries minister put himself in a “brutal” conflict of interest when he stayed in a castle, then a “luxury” shooting lodge — all on the dime of an aquaculture company — during a trip to Scotland last June.
NDP sees ‘brutal’ conflict of interest; O’Driscoll says commissioner OK’ed travel

Newfoundland and Labrador’s NDP says the province’s fisheries minister put himself in a "brutal" conflict of interest when he stayed in a castle, then a "luxury" shooting lodge — all on the dime of an aquaculture company — during a trip to Scotland last June.

Most of Loyola O’Driscoll’s travel to the Aquaculture U.K. conference, including airline tickets and hotel accommodations at the beginning and end of the trip, was paid for by the provincial government.
But after a brief stint at the conference in Glasgow, the minister embarked on a two-night "familiarization" tour of aquaculture sites paid entirely by sea products giant MOWI Scotland.

O’Driscoll’s itinerary for the entire trip, obtained through access to information legislation, shows that on June 16, the minister stayed at the Cameron House, billed on its website as a "luxury Loch Lomond hotel."

The following night, after being ferried to the isolated Isle of Muck, the minister stayed in the Gallanach Lodge, described as a "luxury catered accommodation" with "magical views across the sea to Rum, Canna and Skye."
On the left, the Cameron House, "luxury hotel" located on Loch Lomond. On the right, the Gallanach Lodge, a "luxury catered accommodation" on the Isle of Muck. (Cameron House; Gallanach Lodge)
O'Driscoll's department said it could provide no "value/record" of the travel arrangements, which were made directly by the company.

One night at the Cameron House Loch Lomond, for the same date as the minister stayed but in 2027, would cost at least £429 (about $800), according to the hotel’s website. The Gallanach Lodge’s site shows that a room including breakfast and dinner costs £185 per night (about $350).
‘I had no idea what the accommodations were’

O’Driscoll’s department confirmed that "travel and accommodations and associated expenses" were paid for by MOWI, but stressed that "permission was granted" by Commissioner of Legislative Standards Ann Chafe prior to the trip.
"I had no idea what the accommodations were," O’Driscoll said in an interview, despite the itinerary for his trip clearly listing the names of the hotels at which he stayed.

"We were over there to get more knowledge on the aquaculture industry. I would say personally, before we even went, I called the commissoner of legislative standards to make sure that this is open and transparent and that there would be no issues with what I was doing when I went over there."
In this photo uploaded to Facebook by O'Driscoll's departure, the minister meets with MOWI workers in Scotland. (Department of Fisheries and Aquaculture)

Chafe, whose office oversees MHA ethics, confirmed by email that "approval to accept this sponsored travel was given to the minister following the filing of the full details with this office before leaving to attend the Aquaculture U.K. conference."

Like Chafe, a spokesperson for O’Driscoll’s department said "proper procedures were followed" and that the minister submitted an addendum to his yearly public disclosure statement following his trip, as required by a section of the House of Assembly Act on "accepting extra benefits."

The act states that MHAs may only accept gifts or personal benefits "received as an incident of the protocol or social obligations that normally accompany the duties or responsibilities of office." They may only receive third-party reimbursements for "reasonable travel and associated expenses incurred in performing services that are in the public interest."

For gifts over $500 and for any external travel reimbursement, MHAs must disclose the amount, the source of the gift or money, and a description of the circumstances under which the benefit was received.
Fisheries and Aquaculture Minister Loyola O'Driscoll holds a salmon during a sponsored trip to MOWI fish farms in Scotland. (Department of Fisheries an Aquaculture)

The disclosure addendum O'Driscoll submitted to the commissioner, which can only be viewed in person by visiting Chafe’s office in St. John’s, indicates that the minister received "sponsored/supported" travel to aquaculture sites while in Scotland last June.
However, the document does not give the name of the company that paid for the travel. It also doesn’t provide the value of the travel.
Radio-Canada asked Chafe to provide an estimate for the sponsored travel O’Driscoll received. She did not provide that information.
'I'm sorry, it's brutal'
The provincial New Democrats said regardless of the commissioner’s decision, the minister put himself in a flagrant conflict of interest.
"I’m sorry, it’s brutal," said NDP Leader Jim Dinn, whose last election campaign focused heavily on strengthening ethics rules for provincial politicians.

"We know the controversy around aquaculture in this province, but we also know that government is also the regulator of this industry, making sure that standards are followed," Dinn said. "It's kind of hard to be that regulator when you're accepting these gifts from the very companies you're trying to regulate."
Newfoundland and Labrador NDP Leader Jim Dinn. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
Perception of conflict, despite commissioner’s decision?

"When they were in opposition, this is the very thing that the PCs railed against," said Dinn, pointing to a controversy involving former Liberal premier Andrew Furey’s 2021 trip to a fishing lodge owned by then-billionaire John Risley.

Risley, present for part of Furey’s stay according to news outlet AllNewfoundlandLabrador, announced a major wind-hydrogen development on Newfoundland’s west coast about half a year later, following a decision by the province to lift a long-time moratorium on onshore wind projects.

The Progressive Conservatives, then in Opposition, pounced on the posh fishing trip and filed a complaint with the legislative standards commissioner. Chafe eventually ruled Furey didn’t break any rules.
"Now we're here in this situation and [the PCs] are doing, basically doing, the same thing that they lambasted the Liberals for," Dinn said.
"It's not only important to do right, but to be perceived as doing right, as well," he said.

Asked directly whether he believed an aquaculture company paying for a fisheries minister’s accommodations at a castle and a shooting lodge could create the perception of a conflict of interest, O’Driscoll said: "I don’t think so."
"When I went to the commissioner of legislative standards that's what my intention was, to make sure it was perceived right, transparent and that there were no concerns to me," he said.
